title: UK Study Visa Refusal Rate Hits 6.4%, Highest in Over a Decade
excerpt: Home Office data for the year to September 2026 show refusals more than doubling in a year, withdrawals up nearly fivefold in the peak quarter, and credibility interviews failing four in five applicants called.
body:
• The UK sponsored study visa refusal rate reached 6.4% in the year to September 2026 — the highest rolling rate since the year ending September 2015, and more than double the 3.1% of a year earlier.
  • Withdrawals jumped to 3,682 applications in July-September 2026, against 779 in the same quarter last year, as universities pulled offers before decisions.
  • The PIE News reported last week that 79% of the 11,415 applicants called to a credibility interview between May and October were judged non-credible.
  • For Indian applicants: Home Office data for the first quarter of 2026 put India's refusal rate at 7%, against 1% for applicants from China and the US — preparation for the credibility interview is now the decisive step.

The refusal rate for UK sponsored study visas has reached 6.4% in the year to September 2026, the highest rolling rate since the year ending September 2015, according to analysis of Home Office data by Higher Insights and The Admit, reported by The PIE News. It is the first time the rolling rate has been above 5% since the year to June 2016.

Who is affected

The figures cover sponsored study visas — the Student route used by international students, including dependants — across all nationalities. The rise is broad rather than driven by one country: excluding China, whose applicants are refused at very low rates, the rolling refusal rate rises to 8.2%. Earlier Home Office data for January to March 2026, reported by Times Higher Education, put the refusal rate for Indian applicants at 7%, against 1% for China and the US, 21% for Nigeria and 39% for Pakistan.

How fast it changed

The rolling refusal rate has risen every quarter: 3.8% in the year to December 2025, 4.4% to March 2026 and 4.9% to June 2026, before reaching 6.4% in the year to September. In the July-September quarter alone, the refusal rate was 3.4%, double the 1.7% recorded in the same quarter of 2025 and the highest for a third quarter since 2016.

Withdrawals have risen even faster. In July to September 2026, 3,682 applications were withdrawn before a decision, against 779 in the same period last year. Q3 is the UK's biggest window for issuing visas ahead of the autumn intake, and withdrawals typically mean a university has pulled a place — often because it doubts the application will succeed. Demand fell at the same time: there were 230,300 sponsored study visa applications from main applicants in the quarter, 16% fewer than a year earlier, and visas issued in the quarter fell 17% to 227,668.

The mechanism: credibility interviews and the 5% line

Two pressures sit behind the numbers. The first is the credibility interview, in which a caseworker tests whether an applicant genuinely intends to study. The PIE News reported last week that 79% of the 11,415 applicants called to a credibility interview between May and October were judged non-credible.

The second is the compliance line universities themselves now face. Since June 1, 2026, every student sponsor has been required to keep its own visa refusal rate under 5% under the Home Office's Basic Compliance Assessment, as The Admit has explained. With the sector-wide rate now at 6.4%, universities have a direct incentive to withdraw applications they judge risky before a refusal is recorded against them — one reason withdrawals are climbing faster than refusals.

What to do next

For students applying now, the data point to preparation rather than panic. The credibility interview is the step that decides most refused cases, so applicants should be ready to explain, in their own words, why they chose their course, why that university, and how the qualification fits their plans after graduation. Choosing a sponsor with a strong compliance record also matters, because a university close to its 5% line is more likely to withdraw an offer late in the process.

The Russell Group, which represents research-intensive universities, said it was "watching the sudden rise in visa refusal rates closely". "A robust immigration system is in everyone's interests, but decisions must be fair and transparent, and we should be careful not to deter genuine students in the process," said Zaid Kadhum, the group's policy manager.

The figures were released alongside ONS data showing UK net migration fell to 77,000 in the year to June 2026, down from a record high of 944,000 in 2023. Non-EU arrivals for study-related reasons fell by 33,000 compared with the year to June 2025.
